record.paper_title: Opportunities and open questions in modern β decay
record.context_brief: Novel detector technologies for precision beta decay
record.original_question: How can Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy, quantum-sensor recoil spectroscopy, Superconducting Tunnel Junction detectors, and high-efficiency atom or ion traps be combined or developed to overcome detector non-linearities, backscattering, bremsstrahlung losses, and simulation-validation limits in future precision beta-decay searches for exotic physics?

evidence.quote: Measurements using traditional scintillator or semiconductor technology have carried progress over many decades but face hard-to-avoid systematic uncertainties such as detector non-linearities, backscattering effects and bremsstrahlung losses.
Novel techniques such as Cyclotron Resonance Emission Spectroscopy, however, sidestep many of these systematic uncertainty and promise to bring significant gains in precision.
In the future, a combination of these technologies with high efficiency atom and ion traps hold great potential to further strengthen and diversify the exotic physics reach.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Precision measurements of nuclear beta decay aim to detect signatures of physics beyond the Standard Model by characterizing the energy and angular distributions of emitted electrons (or positrons), recoiling daughter nuclei, and any accompanying neutrals. Traditional scintillator and semiconductor electron spectrometers are limited by three principal sources of systematic uncertainty: (i) detector non-linearities in the energy response, (ii) electron backscattering from detector surfaces, and (iii) bremsstrahlung energy losses in source and detector materials; additionally, the validation of Monte Carlo simulations modeling these effects is limited by available calibration data.

Several emerging detection technologies aim to circumvent these limitations:

1. Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy (CRES): measures the frequency of cyclotron radiation emitted by a charged particle gyrating in a uniform magnetic field B, with frequency ω = eB/(γ m_e), thereby inferring its Lorentz factor γ and kinetic energy non-destructively.

2. Quantum-sensor recoil spectroscopy: uses cryogenic calorimetric sensors (e.g., transition-edge sensors, magnetic microcalorimeters) to measure the kinetic energy of the recoiling daughter ion or atom with eV-scale resolution.

3. Superconducting Tunnel Junction (STJ) detectors: cryogenic devices in which deposited energy breaks Cooper pairs, providing high-resolution spectroscopy of low-energy particles.

4. High-efficiency atom or ion traps: confine the parent nucleus in a near-massless, near-backing-free environment, enabling clean coincidence detection of the beta particle and recoil daughter.

Problem. Design a conceptual experimental scheme that integrates two or more of the above techniques (CRES, quantum-sensor recoil spectroscopy, STJ detectors, atom/ion traps) into a single coincidence apparatus for precision beta-decay measurements (e.g., a measurement of the beta-neutrino angular correlation coefficient a_βν, the Fierz interference term b, or related observables sensitive to scalar/tensor exotic currents). The scheme should (a) eliminate or dramatically reduce the dominant systematic uncertainties of traditional spectrometers (detector non-linearities, backscattering, bremsstrahlung losses), (b) provide internal calibration channels that constrain Monte Carlo simulation uncertainties at the level required for a fractional sensitivity to exotic couplings below 10^{-3}, and (c) achieve a usable rate and acceptance compatible with statistics-limited operation. Quantify expected systematic budgets and identify the technological developments required to realize such a combined apparatus.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a forward-looking experimental program rather than a mathematically posed conjecture. Active R&D efforts (e.g., Project 8 for CRES, He6-CRES, BeEST for STJ, and various MOT/Paul-trap based beta-decay experiments such as TRINAT, WISArD, and St. Benedict) are ongoing as of 2026, but no integrated apparatus combining these technologies at the precision required for definitive exotic-physics searches has been demonstrated. The question therefore remains open.

status_evidence.title: Project 8 / CRES status
status_evidence.snippet: Project 8 continues development of CRES for tritium beta-decay neutrino-mass measurements; no exotic-coupling combined apparatus yet realized.
status_evidence.claim: CRES technology is still in development for precision beta spectroscopy.

status_evidence.title: He6-CRES collaboration
status_evidence.snippet: He6-CRES applies CRES to 6He and 19Ne beta spectra to constrain Fierz term b; ongoing program.
status_evidence.claim: Combination of CRES with exotic-physics beta-decay searches is a current, unresolved R&D effort.

status_evidence.title: BeEST experiment (STJ detectors)
status_evidence.snippet: Superconducting tunnel junction detectors used in 7Be electron capture to probe heavy neutral leptons.
status_evidence.claim: STJ-based recoil spectroscopy is an active, ongoing technique.

status_evidence.title: TRINAT and atom-trap beta decay
status_evidence.snippet: Magneto-optical traps enable backing-free beta-recoil coincidence measurements; precision continues to improve.
status_evidence.claim: Atom/ion traps for beta decay are an active development direction.
